pests.name: Wheat Aphids (various species, e.g., Sitobion avenae)
symptoms: clusters of small soft-bodied insects on leaves, stems, and ear heads
yellowing or reddening of leaves
sticky honeydew leading to sooty mold growth
stunted or distorted growth in seedlings
reduced grain fill when infestation occurs during ear emergence

favorable_conditions.notes: Populations build fastest in mild, dry conditions; heavy rain suppresses numbers. Also a vector for Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus.

ipm_steps: Monitor fields regularly, especially from tillering through ear emergence
Conserve natural predators such as ladybird beetles, lacewings, and parasitic wasps
Delay sowing slightly where regionally appropriate to reduce autumn aphid colonization and virus transmission
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, which favors aphid reproduction
Apply insecticide only if populations exceed local economic thresholds, favoring selective products that spare natural enemies

diseases.name: Stripe Rust / Yellow Rust (Puccinia striiformis)
symptoms: narrow yellow-orange stripes of powdery pustules running parallel to leaf veins
pustules rub off as an orange-yellow powder on fingers or clothing
premature yellowing and drying of leaves
shriveled grain and reduced yield in severe infections
symptoms often start in patches within the field before spreading

favorable_conditions.notes: Favored by cool, humid weather with dew; spreads rapidly via wind-dispersed spores over long distances.

ipm_steps: Plant resistant or tolerant wheat varieties recommended for the region
Monitor fields closely during cool, humid periods, especially early in the season
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which increases susceptibility
Apply fungicide promptly if disease is detected early and weather favors spread, per local extension recommendations
Destroy volunteer wheat plants that can carry the pathogen between seasons

diseases.name: Leaf Rust / Brown Rust (Puccinia triticina)
symptoms: small round to oval orange-brown pustules scattered irregularly on leaves (not in stripes)
pustules rub off as orange-brown powder
yellowing of surrounding leaf tissue as infection progresses
premature leaf drying and reduced grain weight in severe cases

favorable_conditions.notes: Favored by moderate temperatures with periods of leaf wetness from dew or rain.

ipm_steps: Use resistant wheat varieties where available
Scout fields regularly during grain filling stages
Avoid dense planting and excess nitrogen, both of which favor disease spread
Apply fungicide if disease pressure is high and weather remains favorable for spread
Remove volunteer wheat that can harbor the pathogen between seasons

diseases.name: Powdery Mildew (Blumeria graminis)
symptoms: white to grayish powdery fungal growth on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes ears
yellowing of leaf tissue beneath the powdery patches
patches may later develop small black fungal fruiting bodies
reduced photosynthesis and stunted growth in severe cases

favorable_conditions.notes: Favored by high humidity with moderate temperatures and dense crop canopies with poor air circulation; unlike rusts, does not require free water on leaves.

ipm_steps: Use resistant wheat varieties where available
Avoid overly dense sowing rates to improve air circulation
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, which promotes lush, susceptible growth
Apply fungicide if infection is detected early and conditions favor continued spread
Rotate with non-cereal crops where practical to reduce inoculum buildup

diseases.name: Barley Yellow Dwarf Virus (BYDV)
symptoms: yellowing or reddening of leaf tips progressing toward the base
stunted plant growth and reduced tillering
leaves become stiff and upright with discoloration
poor grain fill and reduced yield
transmitted by aphids, so aphid presence is a strong contextual clue

favorable_conditions.notes: Risk tracks aphid vector activity in mild, dry autumn or spring conditions.

ipm_steps: Control aphid vector populations, since they transmit the virus
Use resistant or tolerant wheat varieties where available
Adjust sowing dates where regionally appropriate to avoid peak aphid migration periods
Remove volunteer cereal plants that can harbor both virus and vector between seasons
Monitor early growth stages closely, since early infection causes the most yield loss
